summary: Revisits the Chinese Lottery attack, a massively parallel cryptanalysis effort, and looks at Internet-based versions of it and their potentially serious consequences. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Imagine a million people each trying a few keys on a lock. This memo looks at how the internet could be used to break secret codes that way, and why that matters.

questions: how could a worm crack des
what is the chinese lottery attack
how fast could des be cracked in 2002
why is des no longer used
subtitle: How internet worms could crack encryption by brute force

tldr.problem: DES encryption, which protected many secrets, uses a 56-bit key that can be brute-forced by trying 2 to the 56th power of possibilities. In 1991, this seemed impossible, but the Internet has grown to 100 million hosts and computers are 150 times faster.
tldr.mechanism: An internet worm could infect millions of hosts without being detected, and use them to try DES keys in parallel. Once a winning instance cracks the key, it could report back through hidden web pages, newsgroups, or chat services rather than obviously malicious traffic.
tldr.outcome: Calculations show DES could be cracked in about 1.5 days with 2002-era worms and performance. This threat justified abandoning DES in favor of 3DES and AES, and shows the danger of stealthy, purpose-built malware.

today: RFC 3607 is Informational and documents a threat that was real as of 2003. DES has since been completely phased out, replaced by 3DES and AES. Modern encryption standards have key sizes (128 bits or more) that make brute-force attack computationally infeasible even against a global botnet.

sections.title: The Original Chinese Lottery Attack
sections.content:
In 1991, researchers Quisquater and Desmedt proposed a thought experiment: an attack that uses massively parallel hardware to break DES encryption by brute force. They called it the Chinese Lottery because it resembled a lottery where millions of people each check a few combinations.

The attack was clever but seemed impractical in 1991, when the Internet had only 8 million reachable hosts. However, by 2002, two things had changed dramatically: the Internet grew to 100 million hosts, and desktop computers became about 150 times more powerful. These trends made the thought experiment worth revisiting.
sections.plainLanguage: In 1991, someone had an idea: what if you split a code-cracking job among many computers? It seemed crazy then because there were not many computers. But by 2002, the Internet was huge and computers were much faster.

sections.title: Internet Worms as a Cryptanalytic Tool
sections.content:
Internet worms have proven they can infect hundreds of thousands of machines rapidly and stay hidden. The Code Red v2 worm infected over 350,000 hosts in just 14 hours in 2001. Its payload was mischief—defacing websites. But a worm with a darker purpose, designed to crack an encryption key, could stay hidden far longer because its owner would not want to draw attention.

Such a cryptanalytic worm would use a distributed algorithm: each infected host tries a subset of possible DES keys. When a host finds the correct key, it must contact the worm's creator. However, the creator cannot simply make the worm shout loudly, or the attack would be detected. Instead, the worm could hide the discovered key on compromised websites in an innocuous file with a unique keyword, or post a PGP-encrypted message to newsgroups and IRC channels. The worm's creator would periodically search the Internet or read message boards to retrieve the result.

Even after detection, it would be nearly impossible to determine whose message or encryption was being attacked. The worm would only store one or two pieces of ciphertext and some expected plaintext characteristics, hardly enough to identify the victim.
sections.plainLanguage: A worm could quietly infect millions of computers and use them to try encryption keys. When one finds the answer, it leaves a secret message on a hacked website instead of broadcasting loudly.

sections.title: Performance Projections
sections.content:
Internet growth and computing power follow predictable trends. CPUs roughly double in performance every 1.5 years (Moore's Law), and the Internet population doubles every 3 years. Using a simple model with 1995 as a baseline—when MD5 software achieved 170,000 single-block operations per second and DES achieved 50,000—the RFC calculates what a hypothetical worm could accomplish in any given year.

A key simplifying assumption is that a stealthy worm could maintain a steady-state infection of about 0.5% of all Internet hosts. By 2002, that would be roughly 504,000 infected computers. The calculations showed: DES could be cracked in about 1.45 days, DES with an 8-character password in about 16 minutes, and MD5 with 64-bit keys in about 218 days. However, MD5 with reasonable key lengths was still out of reach.

The memo concludes that a successful attack against DES in 2002 appears to be a near-certainty if an attacker has the resources to build such a worm, making DES unfit for use.
sections.plainLanguage: Doing the math: 500,000 infected computers trying keys in parallel could crack DES in a day or two. That was not science fiction anymore.

sections.title: Security Consequences
sections.content:
DES had already been shown to be weak by specialized hardware attacks, but this memo highlighted a new threat: software-based brute force at scale. The combination of large infected botnets and Moore's Law meant that DES could no longer protect secrets.

The security community responded by abandoning DES in favor of 3DES (which applies DES three times with different keys) and the newer Advanced Encryption Standard (AES), both of which have much larger key sizes and remain secure against brute-force attacks.

The memo also warns that operating systems were becoming more complex and malware authors more sophisticated. Internet worms have historically been used for vandalism, but the same techniques could enable far more dangerous attacks like distributed encryption breaking or data theft. As of February 2003, at least one worm variant (W32/Opaserv.A) had a payload designed to implement a distributed DES cracker, showing that the threat was not merely theoretical.
sections.plainLanguage: People realized DES was broken. They switched to stronger codes like AES. But the memo showed that internet malware was getting smarter and could do attacks that earlier worms could not imagine.
